key_insight: An AI model using wearable sleep and activity data distinguished Parkinson’s disease from healthy controls and detected associated pathological hallmarks; this is not a cancer drug discovery study.
clinical_relevance: Passive wearable monitoring could support future Parkinson’s screening and research cohort enrichment, but clinical use requires further validation.
method: Derived sleep and activity metrics from free-living wrist accelerometry.
Trained SAM-PD to distinguish Parkinson’s disease from healthy controls and tested it independently without retraining.
Compared SAM-PD with the MDS prodromal risk score for detecting dopaminergic deficit and α-synuclein pathology.
evidence_signal: SAM-PD achieved AUROC 0.93 in the U.S. cohort (n=159) and 0.95 in an independent European cohort using a different device (n=40); at-risk cohort AUROCs were 0.86 for dopaminergic deficit and 0.76 for α-synuclein pathology.
watch_item: Small cohorts, particularly the independent validation sample, limit confidence in population-scale screening performance.
paper_title: Wearable-based sleep and activity tracking detects Parkinson's disease and associated pathological hallmarks
